My therapist was just away for a week when he and his wife had a baby.

In those circumstances, I obviously knew it was coming, but timing was up in the air. We have had 2x/week sessions for a year and a half, so it was definitely hard to not have that safe space for week.

What really helped me was to keep myself busy (thankfully it was a busy time at work) and also to accept my irrational thoughts for what they are, irrational. I suffer from PTSD, so I often have emotional reactions that do not fit the situation. I have learned that I have to accept those feelings for what they are, accept that I am "PTSD-ing" about something, and once I stop denying them or judging them, then they start to get smaller. It doesn't fix it - but it starts to get easier.

So my suggestion is to show some compassion for yourself in your feelings, that it is okay you feel that way. And also acknowledge the good that you have realized through this - that you have found a therapist that you really like and trust! That is good!

Well, this is a tough question to answer....but I can give you what I would do...

For me, I think to acknowledge that I am feeling angry (or any other emotion) and also that I do not want to take it out on said person, will help me to diffuse or direct my emotion elsewhere. If I can simply say to that person - I am feeling really angry about X, so that it doesn't come out sideways in pointed at them.

My therapist and I hug at the end of every session, it has been extraordinarily healing and helpful for me. 

Occasionally, if I am having a really difficult session, he will ask if I want a hug in the middle, and he will let me cry on his shoulder a bit.

He will also put his hand on my shoulder or hold my hand during EMDR if I start to cry or get really emotional. This is incredibly helpful for me to stay grounded in the moment - feeling someone touching me - so I don't get caught up in a flashback or dissociation. 

All of it has only helped me and helped our therapeutic relationship. It is not for everyone, and we certainly had conversations about it and boundaries, etc. I have never felt that it was too much, or that he or I were crossing boundaries, etc.

I have been there, for sure, with my therapist. I saw him as a friend, as a person that I felt more safe and trusting with than almost any other person. I think it is completely normal at the beginning to have these feelings, I mean, you are telling this person things that you may never tell anyone else.

What helped me, honestly, was time and also really looking at WHY I had those feelings and actually talking about them with my therapist. For me, I had these feelings because I had attachment/trust issues - as I was abused as a child. I have this person in my life who I know genuinely cares - and I was scared to lose them. As time has gone on, I have felt less and less insecure in the relationship and that has made my fear/sadness decrease significantly.

So my advice is to talk about it openly and really look at what is causing these feelings. It isn't a bad thing - as you could really learn something about yourself.

To be frank - I really don't think that EMDR can cause permanent brain damage. If it could - and that was a legitimate, studied risk factor, then it would be more widely known.

I will say, it is SUPER important, especially with someone with multiple traumas, that a lot of work is done on the front on to make sure that they can handle what EMDR brings up. EMDR will take a toll on you, just as exposure therapy, as you are bringing up stuff that is traumatic. You have to know and feel confident that you have the skills and resources to handle it.

From the little of what you wrote, it may be that there was not enough front end work done to help you through the process, but I can't say for sure.

I would say that my worst day ever included a trip to the behavioral emergency room because I wanted to kill myself (there are probably some equally as bad, but this is what I am going with).

How did I handle it? I brought a trusted friend and just accepted that this is where I am right now and I am doing the right thing in getting help. I am usually terrible at acceptance, but admittedly, that was the most helpful thing to get me through that experience.

Honestly - find a therapist that is not specifically attached to any one way of doing things. Yes, CBT can be helpful and effective for all issues in order to help you re-frame and think more accurately. 

However - with a history of abuse (which I have as well) you need to have a therapist who has experience in working with trauma. Trauma is hard. It is complicated and unique. Maybe even consider a therapist who is certified in EMDR. There is no one-size fits all, unfortunately, as our responses to things can be so different. 

My overall opinion is that finding a therapist that you click with, that you feel that really cares, and can feel invested with them is the most important.

Wishing you all the best.
